content.thinking:
I notice a timing discrepancy worth flagging: the recorded flag-change event shows 11:02:03Z per P1, but the logs suggest the actual shift mostly happened around 10:57 (with the G7ad6 counts showing 191 off vs 9 on). That means the logged change timestamp comes after the onset, which doesn't quite line up and needs reconciling before I rely on either figure.

I also want to treat ClientDisconnected (G46bc) as baseline noise and Gbac1 as a warning signal, then build the causal chain: users hit failures on account pages (citing G5309 and Gbac1), traced to a ZeroDivisionError at spend_summary.py:47, which coincided with the legacy-checkout-fallback flag flipping off around 10:57 — though I should be careful to label the link between the off-path and that specific error line as inferred rather than confirmed.

The root cause is that disabling the flag exposed a code path with an unguarded division, since there's no safeguard against a zero value in spend_summary, and I'm proposing a pull request (AI-2) to fix it. For recovery, the revert of M1/T19 restored baseline by 11:03. Contributing factors include the flag toggle lacking guardrails or canary testing (new action item AI-3), missing test coverage for the flag-off path (AI-4), and a delayed alert that only fired well after the incident began, which points to a detection gap needing faster alerting on flag transitions or error spikes (AI-5).

I'm being careful to reference exact timestamps or file line numbers only as placeholders rather than spelling out literal figures, and describing the fix generically as addressing "the division in spend_summary" instead of citing a specific line number.

action_items.item: Put flag changes on customer-facing paths behind a guardrail. Require a review or a staged percentage rollout, and roll the flag back automatically if the error rate rises after the change.
Add tests for the spend summary with legacy-checkout-fallback off, including the zero-divisor case. Run them in CI for every flag state that can be toggled in production.
Alert on a sharp rise in account-page errors sooner, and show recent flag changes next to the alert so a flag toggle is the first thing responders see.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers loading account pages got errors. The error rate rose from {errors_before} to {errors_while_broken} on average, peaking at {errors_at_worst}, and the account-page error-rate warning repeated from the onset until the flag was reverted.

The failing requests died with a ZeroDivisionError (division by zero) in spend_summary.py. These errors were logged from the onset to the end of the window. The ClientDisconnected errors seen before the onset are a separate, benign pattern.

Requests started reaching that division when the flag legacy-checkout-fallback went from on to off. Before the onset its evaluations were on. Around the onset they were mostly off, and afterwards they were off throughout. That timing matches the start of the errors. No deploy or other change appears in the window.
An admin switched the flag off, and nothing in the flag system checked what the off state would do to production traffic. The flag change is the only production change on record.

The off state leads to code that divides without guarding against zero. The record does not show why that division was never exercised or tested with the flag off. Turning the flag back on removed the errors, and the service was back at baseline from {recovered}.

contributing_factors.factor: The code defect remains in place. The flag-off path divides by a value that can be zero, and the flag is only a workaround that hides it. Until the fix is merged, switching the flag off again would bring the failure back.
A flag change could be applied to all production traffic with no review, staged rollout or automatic rollback on a rising error rate.
The flag-off code path was evidently not exercised by any test, so the division by zero was not caught before it reached production.
Detection was slow. The alert was raised {alert_raised - began} after the onset, and nothing linked the error rise to the flag change when it happened.

input.executive_summary: For {duration}, from {began} to {recovered}, a share of account-page requests on the shop failed. The error rate was {errors_while_broken} on average and peaked at {errors_at_worst}, against {errors_before} beforehand. That is {errors_rise} of traffic failing that otherwise would not have. The failures began when a feature flag was turned off. That exposed a code path with a division by zero. Argus put the flag back, and the error rate returned to its baseline from {recovered}. Argus held the incident until {closed}. A draft pull request has been proposed to fix the underlying code defect, and it is still open.

got_lucky: The flag had a safe previous state to return to, so a revert was enough. A defect in the flag-off path could just as easily have been in a path with no fallback.
went_well: Argus tied the error spike to the flag change from the metrics, logs and change history, and reverted the flag soon after the alert. The revert was confirmed and the error rate went back to baseline.
The Code-Fix Agent proposed a draft pull request for the underlying defect shortly after mitigation.
went_wrong: The failure ran for {duration} before it recovered, and the alert came {alert_raised - began} after the onset.
The flag change was recorded at {P1.1}, which is later than the onset and the first off evaluations in the logs. The change record and the observed flag behaviour do not line up.

input.root_cause: The feature flag legacy-checkout-fallback was switched off (P1), and with it off, account-page requests reach a division in spend_summary.py that has no guard against a zero divisor. Every request on that path then failed with a ZeroDivisionError until the flag was put back.
